content.text: The waves in winter arrive with less patience and more insistence, as though they too were cold. A well-worn path through a wood is a kind of quiet agreement among everyone who uses it. The morning fog burned off by nine most days, later on the days it mattered least.

I burn driftwood because it is what the shore provides, and because it burns with a colour nothing else quite manages. An old friend's handwriting is recognisable at a glance, long after the face has grown less familiar. The market square filled slowly and emptied all at once, as though on a signal no one gave aloud.

A path across the dunes disappears under the first real snow and reappears, unhurried, sometime in March. A garden gate left open is, more often than not, simply an invitation no one has withdrawn. The lamp oil was rationed that winter, and the evenings grew, by necessity, quieter for it.

The winter coast keeps fewer visitors and, I think, more honest ones. An old ledger, found later, tells a fuller story than the person who kept it ever meant to leave behind. The wind changed direction twice in a single afternoon, which the fishermen took as its own kind of warning.

I have walked the shingle at every hour of a December day and found the four in the afternoon light the hardest to describe. A long winter makes the first warm day feel larger than the weather alone accounts for. The workshop's apprentices came and went, but the smell of the place never really changed.

A small fire needs tending more than it needs fuel, which is a lesson that took me longer than it should have. An orchard in bloom is briefly, almost embarrassingly, more beautiful than it has any right to be. The evening post brought less news than expected and somehow felt heavier for it.

The cold has a way of narrowing a person's thoughts down to the essential handful, and I do not always mind that. A house passed down through a family keeps, in its floors and doorframes, a record no deed can match. The harbor at first light belonged to the gulls and the earliest of the fishing boats.

Snow on the dunes holds footprints longer than snow anywhere else I have walked, out of some trick of the wind. An old debt of kindness is rarely called in outright, only quietly remembered. The bread rose slowly in the cold kitchen, and the whole house smelled the better for waiting.

By the shortest day the light lasts barely long enough to walk the headland and back before dark overtakes it. A traveller's stories improve with each telling, a fact both teller and listener quietly agree to overlook. The workshop closed for the season the way it always did, mid-sentence, with a job left half finished.

I keep a small fire and a smaller store of patience, and some winters one runs out well before the other. An old road, no longer maintained, is still walkable long after it stops being useful. The frost patterns on the window that January were, by common agreement, the finest anyone could recall.

The coast in December does not ask to be admired, which is, I have decided, part of what I admire about it. A letter home, written honestly, is harder to write than any other kind. The village kept its own time, twenty minutes behind the railway, and saw no reason to change.

Walking alone teaches you the sound of your own breathing in a way company never quite allows. An empty ledger page is, in its way, as informative as a full one. The last apple of the season always tasted, everyone agreed, a little better for being the last.

A winter meditation, if it is honest, ends without a conclusion, only a walk back toward the fire. A long friendship survives more silence than most people think it can. The workshop lamp burned oil at a rate its owner tracked more carefully than his own accounts.

The tide in December comes in grey and leaves grey, and I have learned not to expect it to announce a mood. An old map, however wrong, still tells you what someone once believed to be true. The harbor bell rang for fog more nights that year than anyone could remember from before.

A small fire against the dark is not much of an argument, but it is the only one available most winter nights. A garden planted in hope outlives, more often than not, the gardener's doubts about it. The evening chores went faster with two people than with one, though neither said so aloud.

Walking alone in snow teaches a particular kind of attention, since every sound behind you might be the only one for miles. An old coat pocket, searched later, tells you where its owner had actually been. The workshop's youngest apprentice asked more questions than the others combined, and was rarely told to stop.

I have come to think the coast in winter tells the truth more often than the coast in summer bothers to. A river in flood forgives nothing and remembers everything, at least until the next flood. The last light in the house went out later that winter than in any winter before it.

The gulls that stay through December earn a grudging respect from the ones who do not. An unopened letter waits with a patience its writer rarely shared. The bakery's ovens stayed warm long after closing, heating the whole street a little further into the evening.

A single lit window across the bay becomes, by February, a fixed point I check for before I check anything else. A long-kept promise is worth more, if anything, for having been long-kept. The harbor emptied of boats by storm warning and filled again, cautiously, the following noon.

Meditation, out here, is mostly just cold feet and a willingness to keep walking regardless. An old friend recognized across a crowded market is a small, entirely disproportionate joy. The workshop's ledgers, taken together, told a quieter story than either the profits or the losses alone.

A garden wall built by hand outlasts, as a rule, the hands that built it. Time moves at a different pace when there is work enough to fill it entirely. A room remembers its last occupant longer than most people expect.

The kettle took its usual three minutes, and in that time the whole morning seemed to settle. Distance is measured in more than miles once you have walked enough of it yourself. A garden left untended for a season still remembers, mostly, what it was planted to become.

The clock in the hall ran two minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and no one corrected it. Patience is easier to recommend than to practise, a fact every teacher of it eventually admits. The correspondence between old friends thins with distance but rarely stops outright.

A machine well maintained will forgive a great many small mistakes; one neglected forgives none. Quiet, in the right house, is not an absence of sound but a particular kind of company. The weather that season did exactly what the almanac predicted, which surprised everyone involved.

A long walk clarifies more than a long conversation, in my limited experience of both. The light in late afternoon has a habit of making ordinary rooms look briefly important. Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential.

A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it. The city at that hour belonged mostly to delivery carts and the occasional insomniac. Old letters, reread, always sound slightly more confident than the person who wrote them actually was.
